new_statements.quote: Normal Muyang speech applies relatively great stress to the final syllable of an utterance. This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length ... Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. [...] Amplitude and high tone in Muyang are linked. [...] It may be, therefore, that if stress is relevant at word-level at all, it is closely linked to tone. Nouns of two syllables starting with high tone have a tendency to break the link between tone and amplitude, suggesting that there may be an overriding tendency towards word-final stress in disyllabic nouns. [...] With the exception of the utterance-final increase, stress in general may not prove to be a significant factor in Muyang.
new_statements.citation: Smith, Tony. 1999. Muyang Phonology. Yaoundé: SIL / Ministry of Scientific and Technical Research, Cameroon.
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement

This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length - almost equivalent to doubling the length of the vocalisation of a final syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Muyang is a tone language (three surface level tones H/M/L, perhaps two underlying). Prominence (amplitude and especially length) falls on the final syllable of the utterance, which masks any word-level pattern in citation forms; within nouns amplitude tracks High tone, with a possible tendency to word-final stress in disyllabic nouns; the author concludes stress is probably not a significant independent factor at word level, pending further research.
new_statements.exceptions: Utterance-final stress overrides the tone-amplitude correlation (a word-final Low gets more force than preceding Highs); disyllabic H-initial nouns tend toward word-final stress; remarks based only on recorded nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: The firm statement is utterance/phrase-level (final syllable of the utterance); word-level stress explicitly left undetermined. Isolation (citation) forms show the utterance-final lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: Smith 1999 describes Muyang as spoken in Guduba (canton of Palbara), Tokombéré, Mayo-Sava, Far North Cameroon; same language as Glottolog muya1243, no dialect split noted. The stress remarks are explicitly 'based on a brief study of recorded data for nouns'.

sources.quote: Normal Muyang speech applies relatively great stress to the final syllable of an utterance. This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length ... Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. [...] Amplitude and high tone in Muyang are linked. [...] It may be, therefore, that if stress is relevant at word-level at all, it is closely linked to tone. Nouns of two syllables starting with high tone have a tendency to break the link between tone and amplitude, suggesting that there may be an overriding tendency towards word-final stress in disyllabic nouns. [...] With the exception of the utterance-final increase, stress in general may not prove to be a significant factor in Muyang.
sources.note: Ch. 5 'Stress' (p.30): utterance-final syllable receives great stress (amplitude, ~doubled length), so a word's own stress pattern is not observable in isolation; in nouns amplitude correlates with High tone; disyllabic nouns show a tendency to word-final stress; concludes stress 'may not prove to be a significant factor', word-level stress not yet established. Ch. 4: three surface level tones H, M, L (possibly two underlying).
